title: Predictive warmup and cost smoothing playbook for private deployments
author: Priya Malhotra
body:
Summary:

This playbook describes a practical, operator-friendly approach to reducing cold-start latency and smoothing incremental cost in private Redwood deployments by using predictive warmup, staged prefetching, tenant-prioritized warmers, and coordinated rollback behaviors. It complements the cold-start latency mitigation guidance by giving an operational recipe for scheduling warmup work, validating its effectiveness, and safely reverting or throttling warmers when load, cost, or telemetry signals indicate risk.

Scope:
- Applies to VPC and on-prem Redwood Private installations running model-serving runtime v2.6+ with background-job workers enabled.
- Focuses on inference warmup (KV-cache and kernel priming) and transient prefetching of token prefixes for high-impact tenants or endpoints.
- Not a replacement for capacity planning; intended to bridge gaps where short-lived bursts or predictable schedules cause poor tail latency and variable unit-cost.

When to use:
- Customers reporting intermittent 95th/99th pct latency regressions tied to cold-starts (e.g., nightly workflows, batch-to-online cutovers).
- Deploys where on-demand autoscale is slow due to provisioning time or constrained GPU availability.
- To reduce unit-cost variance for billing-sensitive tenants by avoiding repeated cold allocations.

Key concepts and definitions:
- Warmup job: a lightweight background job that issues controlled inference requests to pre-populate KV cache + allocator data structures and to warm CUDA kernels (small prefix lengths).
- Predictive warmup: scheduling warmup jobs based on expected future traffic (cron, forecast from telemetry or customer-supplied schedule).
- Cost smoothing: intentionally shifting small amounts of compute from high-price, bursty periods into predictable pre-warm windows to avoid expensive on-demand spikes.
- Safety fences: limits and circuit-breakers preventing warmup jobs from causing capacity starvation or billing spikes.

Design principles:
1) Tenant-aware: warmers operate per-tenant or per-route so they respect quotas and isolation boundaries.
2) Conservative resource footprint: jobs use reduced batch sizes, short sequences, low concurrency (e.g., 1–4 concurrent warmers per GPU).
3) Observable and reversible: warmers emit telemetry (warmup.start/finish, memory delta, KV-hits % increase) and are controlled by feature flags and scheduler policies.
4) Predictive but auditable: forecasts should be backed by telemetry windows (historical schedule) or signed customer-supplied calendars.

Warmup strategies and examples:
- Scheduled pre-warm: cron-driven warmup 5–15 minutes before known traffic (e.g., business-hours cutover). Use for steady predictable workloads.
- Windowed burst warmup: monitor request rate derivative; when rate increases beyond ramp threshold, spawn a bounded set of warmers and dissolve when derivative drops.
- Rolling warmers for model swap: when a new model version is promoted, run warmers across a staged subset of nodes to prime kernels and KV cache before traffic is routed.
- Passive opportunistic warmup: piggyback warmup across low-priority background work (index refresh, telemetry aggregation) to avoid dedicated warm cycles.

Operational configuration (recommended defaults):
| config | recommended default | notes |
|---|---:|---|
| max_warmers_per_gpu | "4" | hard cap to prevent starvation |
| warmup_batch_size | "8" | tune downward for <A100-80GB> constrained environments |
| warmup_sequence_len | "32" | short prefix to exercise attention kernels |
| warmup_concurrency | "2" | concurrent threads per operator-worker |
| cost_smoothing_window_minutes | "60" | moving window to amortize warm cost |
| budget_pct_of_daily_cpu | "2" | percentage of reservable compute for warmers |

Example scheduler YAML (to include in operator deployments):

# warmup-scheduler.yaml (example)
# This fragment configures the predictive warmup controller
controller: warmup-controller
policies:
  - name: daily-business-hour-prewarm
    trigger: cron
    cron: "0 8 * * 1-5"
    target_tenants: ["tenant:acme-commerce", "tenant:ux-bot"]
    concurrency: 2
    sequence_len: 64
    budget_pct: 1
  - name: ramp-detect-prefetch
    trigger: telemetry-derivative
    threshold_requests_per_min: 50
    lookback_minutes: 5
    max_scale: 3
    decay_minutes: 10

Metrics and observability (must be present):
- warmup.jobs.started (counter, labels: tenant, route, model_version)
- warmup.jobs.succeeded / failed (counter)
- warmup.kv_hit_increase (gauge, percent) — measured pre/post warmup on node-local cache
- warmup.memory_delta_mb (gauge) — increase in GPU DRAM or reserved device memory
- warmup.cpu_seconds (counter) — background CPU consumed
- warmup.cost_estimate_usd (gauge) — approximate cost assigned to warm job (for billing reconciliation)
Dashboards should include: warmup success rates, 95th/99th latency delta with/without warmup, warmup cost vs. saved spikes (estimated).

Safety and circuit breakers:
1) Global budget enforcement: aggregate warmup cost for the rolling window must be < configured budget_pct_of_daily_cpu or else the controller reduces concurrency by 50%.
2) Memory pressure abort: if warmup.memory_delta_mb + node.memory_used > node.memory_threshold (default 85%), abort further warmers on that node and emit alert.
3) Latency tailbackoff: if p99 latency increases during warmup window (vs. baseline) by > 15%, automatically stop warmers and mark the tenant policy as failed.
4) Billing cap: per-tenant warmup cost must be capped; customers may opt-in to higher budgets with an SLA amendment.

Rollout and validation checklist (operator steps):
1) Stage configuration in a canary namespace or single low-impact tenant.
2) Verify metrics generation: ensure warmup.jobs.started and warmup.kv_hit_increase appear in the telemetry pipeline.
3) Execute a single scheduled warmup and validate:
   a) KV hit rate increases on the targeted nodes by > 20%.
   b) No memory pressure or OOM events.
   c) Latency for that tenant decreases during first 10 minutes of traffic in a controlled A/B test.
4) Increase concurrency to target defaults while monitoring for regressions for 24h.
5) Enable tenant-prioritization policies and document billing/chargeback flows.

Rollback and remediation playbook:
- Fast-stop: flip the feature-flag warmup.enabled = false to prevent new warmers. Existing warmers will complete or be killed based on policy.
- Drain-and-evict: if memory pressure continues, run node-level: agentctl evict-warmers --node <node-id> --grace 30s.
- Forensic capture: on abort, snapshot the following and attach to incident: warmup job logs, two minute telemetry window for warmup.* metrics, node memory and GPU tracer dump.
- Postmortem signals to evaluate: p99 delta, warmup.jobs.failed rate, cost_estimate_usd total.

Operator CLI recipes (examples):
- Start a one-off warmup for tenant: operatorctl warmup start --tenant acme-commerce --routes "/api/v1/chat" --job-size 2 --seq-len 32
- Check warmup status: operatorctl warmup list --tenant acme-commerce --since 1h
- Abort warmers on node: operatorctl warmup abort --node gpu-12 --reason "memory-pressure"

Ownership and responsibilities:
- Oncall SRE: owns the real-time runbook (alerts, abort criteria, operator commands).
- Runtime team: maintains the warmup-controller and ensures warmers adhere to memory and concurrency APIs.
- Solutions engineering / CS: works with customers to agree warmup budgets and scheduling calendars for cost reconciliation.

Acceptance criteria and SLO impact assessment:
- Target: reduce cold-start-induced p99 latency by >= 30% for scheduled workloads without increasing average token cost by > 5%.
- Emergency threshold: if warmup.jobs.failed rate > 10% in a 30m window, alert P1 and auto-stop scheduled warmups.

Security and compliance notes:
- Warmup requests must not contain or leak customer payload. Use synthetic, policy-compliant prefix inputs or customer-supplied anonymized prefixes under an evidence contract.
- Warmers must use operator-scoped credentials; do not reuse customer API tokens.

Appendix A — Example warmup payload (synthetic):
{
  "input": "<SYN_THERMAL_CHECK> warmup - tokenized prefix for priming attention",
  "max_tokens": 8
}

Appendix B — Quick troubleshooting table:
- Symptom: p99 increases during warmup -> Action: stop warmers, capture telemetry, revert to previous warmup concurrency.
- Symptom: memory pressure OOMs -> Action: decrease warmup_sequence_len and warmup_batch_size, evict warmers on impacted nodes.
- Symptom: warmup cost higher than savings -> Action: measure warmup.cost_estimate_usd and compare to modeled saved-spike cost; revert to conservative scheduled windows.

Related pages and references:

- See tenant-burst-absorber-and-eviction-strategy for complementary burst-handling patterns.
